Faq.title: Your questions, answered.
Faq.subtitle: Quick answers about how we work, our stack and how to start a project.

q1.question: What kind of projects does ByteFlow build?
q1.answer: Websites and landing pages (including WordPress), e-commerce, mobile apps, internal systems and dashboards — from interface design to deploy infrastructure. We also produce videos and motion graphics for promotion.

q2.question: Which technologies do you use?
q2.answer: Mainly TypeScript, React, Next.js, Vue/Nuxt and Node.js, with Prisma and PostgreSQL on the back end, plus Docker, GitHub Actions, AWS and Cloudflare for infrastructure.

q3.question: How long does a project take?
q3.answer: It depends on scope. Once we understand your needs, we send a proposal with defined stages, timeline and deliverables for each phase.

q4.question: Do you maintain existing projects?
q4.answer: Yes. We take over ongoing projects to fix technical debt, improve performance and ship new features, as we did at FutBuyNow.

q5.question: Do you work with agencies (white-label)?
q5.answer: Yes. We act as a partner development team for agencies, delivering the project under the agency’s brand to the end client.

q6.question: How do I start a project with ByteFlow?
q6.answer: Send a message by email or LinkedIn describing your idea. We’ll set up a quick call and come back with scope, recommended stack and timeline.

futbuynow.summary: Ongoing maintenance and evolution of a global FC coins marketplace — performance, internal tooling and automated deploys.

sections.label: Context
sections.text: As a freelancer, I took over the ongoing maintenance and evolution of FutBuyNow, a marketplace for buying and selling FC coins aimed at players worldwide. The product already existed, but had piled up technical debt, performance bottlenecks and a lack of internal tools to analyze and manage the business.

sections.label: Technical approach
sections.text: The work happens in a monorepo with three independent apps — a Node/Express API with Prisma, a React/Vite dashboard and a Next.js store in 16 languages via next-intl. The biggest challenges were optimizing the sitemap, which timed out in production, building dynamic bonus configuration in the admin panel, adding filters to the orders dashboard and integrating Stripe webhooks.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Measurable improvements: CLS dropped from 0.47 to 0.1 and the sitemap endpoint went from timing out to 2.8s in production, with over 1,000 posts. I also set up Docker and GitHub Actions for automated deploys to staging, and shipped dozens of features that made the platform easier to operate.

futcustom.summary: A complete e-commerce for fans to order custom football cards — from real-time customization to after-sales.

sections.label: Context
sections.text: A client needed a platform where fans could order FIFA-style custom football cards with their name, photo and team. The challenge was turning a visual customization flow into a smooth buying experience, with both physical and digital delivery.

sections.label: Stack & decisions
sections.text: The app was built with the Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Prisma and PostgreSQL. Zustand handles real-time customization state and RTK Query handles API calls. Checkout supports PIX and cards (Stripe), shipping is calculated with Melhor Envio, the UI ships in three languages with next-intl, and the funnel is tracked end to end with GTM/GA4 and server-side GTM.

sections.label: Delivery
sections.text: The product was delivered complete — from authentication to after-sales — including an admin panel, a checkout with multiple payment and delivery methods, and the full analytics setup. Architecture decisions were made end to end, from database modeling to the purchase-flow UX.

teflyclass.summary: Academic management platform for ETEJCG, centralizing assignments, projects and announcements with role-based access.

sections.label: Context
sections.text: ETEJCG had no central platform for academic management. Class representatives and students relied on informal group chats to share assignments, projects and announcements, which made information messy and hard to track.

sections.label: Solution
sections.text: I built a system with role-based access control, where class representatives and authorized students publish assignments, projects and announcements in a structured way, keeping that responsibility inside the platform.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: The platform now organizes the school's academic flow, reducing reliance on informal channels and giving students and representatives more visibility and control over each class's tasks.
